desc:
A region has n towns numbered 0 to n - 1 and one-way roads roads[i] = [a, b, w] of length w. A route from town 0 to town n - 1 is any walk along the roads: towns and roads may be used more than once.

Let L be the length of the shortest route. Return the length of the shortest route whose length is strictly greater than L (routes of length exactly L do not count, however many there are). Return -1 if there is no route at all or no route longer than L.

n = 4
roads = [[0,1,1], [1,3,1], [0,2,2], [2,3,2], [1,2,1]]
shortest: 0-1-3 = 2;  next lengths: 0-1-2-3 = 4, 0-2-3 = 4
-> 4
constraints: If n == 1, the only town is both start and end (a route of length 0 always exists)
hints: A plain shortest path only gives you the best length. What extra information per town would let you also know the second best?
Keep two values for every town: the shortest and the second shortest distinct route length that reaches it. A route may revisit towns, so the second best can go around a cycle.

Run Dijkstra on (length, town) entries. When you relax an edge with new length nd, update the first value if nd beats it (the old first value becomes a candidate for the second), otherwise update the second if nd is strictly between the two. Push an entry whenever either value changes.
editorial: Think of each town as two states: 'reached with the best length' and 'reached with the second best distinct length'. A route to town v that is second best must arrive over a last road u -> v whose own route to u was either best or second best, otherwise swapping in a better prefix would give something shorter and still distinct. So it suffices to keep two lengths per town.

Use a Dijkstra loop over (length, town). Pop the smallest entry and skip it when it is longer than the town's second best (it is stale). For every road, compute nd = length + w; if nd < first[v], swap it into first[v] and carry the old first value on as nd; then if first[v] < nd < second[v] set second[v] = nd. Push the entry for each value that changed. Because lengths are positive, entries pop in non-decreasing order and each town is finalised at most twice.

The answer is second[n - 1], or -1 if it stays infinite. Each of the 2V states is expanded once, so the time is O((V + E) log E). For n == 1 the first value is 0 and the second is the shortest cycle through town 0, if any.
